subject: Chemistry
title: Sulfonamides: The First Antibacterials
description: A short lesson to help you apply Sulfonamides: The First Antibacterials.

hook.text: Before penicillin, sulfonamides were the first drugs to fight bacterial infections. They saved thousands in World War II.

buildup.text: In 1932, Gerhard Domagk tested Prontosil, a red dye, on his daughter dying from streptococcal infection. She survived.

discovery.text: Sulfonamides trick bacteria. They mimic a vitamin bacteria need (PABA), blocking the enzyme that uses it. Bacteria starve.

twist.text: The French discovered that only part of Prontosil was active—the sulfonamide fragment. It couldn't be patented. Free for all.

climax.text: Winston Churchill was saved by sulfonamides in 1943 when he developed pneumonia. The drug may have changed WWII's outcome.

punchline.text: A red dye that fooled bacteria. The first antibiotic was a molecular mimic.

quiz.question: How do sulfonamide antibiotics work?
options: They mimic a vitamin bacteria need, blocking a critical enzyme pathway
They dissolve bacterial cell membranes on contact
They inject toxic metals into bacterial cells

details.summary: Sulfonamides, discovered by Gerhard Domagk in 1935, were the first drugs to systematically treat bacterial infections. They work by mimicking para-aminobenzoic acid and competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase.
details.whyItMatters: Sulfonamides saved thousands of lives before penicillin became available and proved that synthetic chemicals could cure infectious diseases. They established the concept of molecular mimicry in drug design.
takeaways: Sulfonamides mimic a bacterial metabolite to block folic acid synthesis
They exploit a metabolic pathway present in bacteria but not humans
Domagk won the 1939 Nobel Prize for discovering their antibacterial action

faq.question: Why do sulfonamides kill bacteria but not human cells?
faq.answer: Bacteria must synthesize their own folic acid using dihydropteroate synthase, which sulfonamides block. Human cells lack this enzyme entirely because humans obtain folic acid from food. This selective toxicity allows sulfonamides to kill bacteria without harming the patient.

faq.question: Are sulfonamides still used in medicine today?
faq.answer: Yes, the combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim remains widely prescribed for urinary tract infections, pneumocystis pneumonia, and MRSA skin infections. While many bacteria have developed resistance, sulfonamides remain important in the antibiotic arsenal for specific infections.
